primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1378943/ (Printed pp. A592 and A566, Green et al and Park et al)
assessment: The randomized ulcerative proctocolitis study uses olive-oil capsules as a placebo and measures bowel symptoms and inflammation. The separate oropharyngeal dysphagia study includes one participant with Parkinson disease and compares gastrostomy with nasogastric feeding using the same formula. Neither presents a dietary EVOO swallowing result.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6453219/ (Kyrgyzstan Mediterranean diet survey and separate transcutaneous stimulation RCT NCT02379182)
assessment: The stroke dietary survey records a preference question about olives and olive oil. A separate poststroke dysphagia trial compares electrical stimulation approaches plus swallowing adaptations. These papers do not measure swallowing after isolated EVOO consumption.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6777611/ (Varret et al PCSK9 postprandial lipid metabolism poster, and separate myotonic dystrophy phenotypes)
assessment: Olive oil gavage is part of a metabolic challenge in transgenic mice and the outcomes are lipids. Dysphagia appears in separate genetic phenotyping, including myotonic dystrophy, without a dietary EVOO swallowing comparison.

Abstract 145 uses olive oil as a vehicle in a liver-regeneration mouse experiment. Abstract 077 reports poststroke dysphagia treated with pharyngeal stimulation in a separate protocol with no dietary EVOO comparator.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1713266/ (Printed index p. 5, Asparagus entry; linked original DOI 10.1136/bmj.281.6256.1676)
assessment: The printed index directs the reader to a human study of the ability to smell urinary metabolites after asparagus intake. The underlying experiment compares detection of odor, without a steamed asparagus or swallowing-difficulty assessment.
